source_text:
Οἱ δὲ κατάδικοι σκοπήσαντες, ποῦ ἀνήχθησαν
ὑπὸ τῶν ἀετῶν τὰ κρέα, ἀπέρχονται, καὶ οὕτω φέρουσι τοὺς λίθους. Ἔχουσι δὲ
ἐνέργειαν τοιάνδε· βαλλόμενοι γὰρ ἐπ' ἀνθράκων πυρὸς, αὐτοὶ μὲν οὐ βλάπτονται,
τοὺς δὲ ἄνθρακας κατασβεννύουσιν.
Οὐ μόνον δὲ τοῦτο, ἀλλὰ καὶ λαμβάνων τις τὸν λίθον, καὶ περιειλίσας ἐν
ὀθόνῃ, τινὶ ἐπιθεὶς ἐπ' ἄνθρακας, κρατῶν αὐτὸν μὲν ἀπὸ τῆς πυρᾶς φλογίζεται, ἡ δὲ
ὀθόνη ἀβλαβὴς μένει, Λέγεται δὲ καὶ ταῖς τικτούσαις γυναιξὶν εὐτοκίας χάριν
χρησιμεύειν. Ἀχάτης ὑποκυανίζων μέν ἐστιν, εὑρίσκεται δὲ καὶ οὗτος περὶ τὰς
Σκυθίας χώρας ἐκείνας. Τριβόμενος δὲ ἐπὶ τῷ μετώπῳ, δήγματος ἀποτρέπει πόνον
σκορπίων τε καὶ ἐχιδνῶν. Ἀμέθυσος φλογίζων μέν ἐστι βαθέως, ἐν δὲ τοῖς ὄρεσιν
εὑρίσκεται Λιβύης πρὸς ταῖς ὄχθαις τῆς θαλάσσης. Χρυσόλιθος χρυσίζων μέν ἐστιν,
εὑρίσκεται δὲ ἐν τῇἈφραίτιδι πέτρᾳ, παρὰ τὸ χεῖλος τῆςἈχεμενίδος Βαβυλῶνος. Τὴν
γὰρ Βαβυλῶνα καὶ τὸ φρέαρ ἐκεῖνο τῆς πέτραςἈχεμενίδα καλοῦσι. Τριβόμενος δὲ,
στοχαστικοῖς (καὶ κωλικοῖς) καὶ κοιλιακοῖς ἰατρικὸς ὑπάρχει. Βηρύλλιον γλαυκίζων
μέν ἐστι, γίνεται δὲ παρὰ τὰ σπέρματα τοῦ ὄρους τοῦ καλουμένου Ταύρου. Ὀνύχιον
ξανθὸν μέν ἐστιν, εὑρίσκεται δὲ καὶ οὗτος ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ ὄρει.
De xii gemmis (fragmenta alia ap. Anastasium Sinaitam, Quaestiones et
responsiones)
Επιφανίου ἐκ τοῦ πρὸς ∆ιόδωρον.
thought_title: The condemned men retrieve the stones; properties of hyacinth, agate, amethyst, chrysolite, beryl, onyx
orientation: Epiphanius continues describing how the condemned men retrieve the hyacinth stones from the ravine, then lists the powers and places of origin of several stones on the breastplate.
pass_a_gloss: But the condemned men, having observed where the meats were carried up by the eagles, go away, and thus they carry the stones. And they have such a power: for when thrown upon coals of fire, they themselves are not harmed, but they quench the coals. And not only this, but also someone taking the stone, and having wrapped it in a linen cloth, having placed it upon coals, while holding it, he himself is burned by the fire, but the linen cloth remains unharmed. And it is said also to be useful to women giving birth for the sake of easy delivery. Agate is somewhat dark blue, and this one also is found around those Scythian regions. And when rubbed on the forehead, it turns away the pain of the bite of scorpions and vipers. Amethyst is deeply fiery, and it is found in the mountains of Libya near the banks of the sea. Chrysolite is golden, and it is found in the Aphraitis rock, beside the lip of Achemenid Babylon. For they call Babylon and that well of the rock Achemenis. And when rubbed, it is medicinal for those who aim at the bowels and for those with colic and for those with intestinal ailments. Beryl is bluish-gray, and it comes to be near the seeds of the mountain called Taurus. Onyx is yellow, and this one also is found in the same mountain.

lemmas.gloss: for those who aim at the bowels

choices.why: The glossary specifies 'power' for δύναμις; here the synonym ἐνέργεια carries the same sense of inherent property, so I render it 'power' to keep the terminology consistent.
The word refers to a fine cloth or linen; 'linen cloth' is literal and clear for a first-time reader.

choices.english: for the sake of easy delivery
choices.why: The phrase means 'for the sake of good childbirth'; 'easy delivery' captures the therapeutic sense plainly.
The verb means 'to be somewhat dark blue'; the prefix ὑπο- indicates a slight or partial quality, so 'somewhat dark blue' is literal.

choices.english: for those who aim at the bowels
choices.why: The adjective στοχαστικός is unusual; it appears to derive from στοχάζομαι, 'to aim at,' and in a medical context likely refers to those aiming at or targeting the bowels. I keep the literal sense with a gloss-like rendering.
rejected: for those who suffer in the bowels

choices.why: The verb γλαυκίζω means 'to be bluish-gray' or 'to have a gray-blue color'; 'bluish-gray' is the standard literal rendering.

pass_b_english: The condemned men observe where the eagles carried the meat, go there, and so bring back the stones. The stones have this power: when thrown onto burning coals, they are not harmed, and they quench the coals.

And not only this, but if someone takes the stone, wraps it in a linen cloth, and places it on the coals, while he holds it, he himself is scorched by the fire, yet the linen cloth remains unharmed. It is also said to help women in labor for the sake of easy delivery.
The agate is somewhat dark blue, and it too is found in those regions of Scythia. When rubbed on the forehead, it turns away the pain of a bite from scorpions and vipers.

The amethyst is deeply fiery, and it is found in the mountains of Libya near the shores of the sea. The chrysolite is golden, and it is found in the Aphraitis rock, beside the edge of Achemenid Babylon. For they call Babylon and that well of the rock Achemenis. When rubbed, it serves as medicine for those with stomach ailments, for those with colic, and for those with intestinal ailments.
The beryl is bluish-gray, and it occurs near the foothills of the mountain called Taurus. The onyx is yellow, and it too is found on the same mountain.
From Epiphanius, from the work addressed to Diodorus.

problems.quote: the hand holding it is scorched by the fire
problems.source_quote: κρατῶν αὐτὸν μὲν ἀπὸ τῆς πυρᾶς φλογίζεται
problems.why: Subject is wrong: κρατῶν (the one holding) refers to the person, not specifically 'the hand'; 'he' is scorched, not 'the hand'.
problems.fix: the one holding it is scorched by the fire from the pyre

problems.quote: those who aim at the bowels
problems.why: στοχαστικοῖς means 'sufferers from dysentery/target-shooters' (a disease term), not 'those who aim at the bowels'.
problems.fix: for dysenterics, for those with colic
problems.ruling: στοχαστικοῖς is a medical term for dysentery sufferers; 'aim at the bowels' mistranslates, misleading readers.

problems.why: στοχαστικοῖς (a corruption of στομαχικοῖς, stomach sufferers) does not mean dysenterics; this substitutes a different medical condition not in the Greek.
problems.ruling: 'Dysenterics' means dysentery; στοχαστικοῖς (emended στομαχικοῖς) means stomach sufferers—not dysentery, and κοιλιακοῖς already covers belly ills.
